title: React.js and Next.js Mastery Question Bank
description: Questions and answers covering React fundamentals, Hooks, rendering, performance, React 19 APIs, Next.js App Router and Pages Router, caching, security, testing, debugging, and architecture scenarios.

questions.question: What problem does React solve?
options: It adds server-side database access to JavaScript applications.
It provides a built-in router and HTTP client for single-page apps.
It lets developers build declarative, component-based user interfaces that update when data changes.
It compiles JavaScript into native mobile applications.
questions.explanation: React reconciles descriptions of UI with the rendered output.

questions.question: What is a component?
options: A reusable unit of UI, commonly a JavaScript function returning React nodes.
A CSS class that styles a section of the page.
A JavaScript object that stores application data.
A server endpoint that returns HTML fragments.
questions.explanation: Components compose into larger interfaces.

questions.question: What is a React element?
options: An immutable description of a UI node, commonly created by JSX.
A mutable DOM node that React updates in place.
A browser event handler attached to a node.
A CSS rule applied to a component.
questions.explanation: An element is not the same thing as a component instance.

questions.question: What is JSX?
options: A template language compiled by the server into HTML strings.
A CSS preprocessor for styling React components.
Syntax for describing UI with XML-like expressions inside JavaScript.
A binary format for serializing component trees.
questions.explanation: Tooling transforms JSX into JavaScript; browsers do not parse JSX directly.

questions.question: What are props?
options: Read-only inputs passed from a parent component.
Mutable values owned and changed by the child component.
Values stored in the browser's local storage.
Functions that run when a component unmounts.
questions.explanation: A new render can receive new props; children should not mutate them.

questions.question: What is state?
options: Component-owned data that persists across renders and can trigger a new render.
Read-only data passed down from a parent component.
Global data shared by every component automatically.
A CSS-in-JS style object attached to a component.
questions.explanation: Use it for values that change and affect UI.

questions.question: What is declarative UI?
options: Writing imperative DOM mutation steps for every change.
Defining components only through class inheritance.
Describing what the UI should look like for current data instead of manually mutating the DOM.
Writing HTML templates that the server fills in.
questions.explanation: React calculates and commits the required updates.

questions.question: What is one-way data flow?
options: Data flows from children to parents through props, and parents notify children with callbacks.
Data flows in both directions automatically between parent and child.
Data typically flows from parents to children through props, while callbacks communicate events upward.
Data is stored globally and read by any component without props.
questions.explanation: It makes state ownership easier to trace.

questions.question: What is component composition?
options: Building larger interfaces by combining smaller components and passing children or slots.
Making components inherit behavior from base classes.
Merging several components' source files into one file.
Duplicating a component's code wherever it is needed.
questions.explanation: It is generally favored over inheritance-heavy designs.

questions.question: What does `children` represent?
options: The renderable content nested inside a component's JSX tags.
The list of CSS classes applied to the component.
The component's internal state object.
The component's return value after rendering.
questions.explanation: It may be text, elements, arrays, or other valid React nodes.

questions.question: What are Fragments?
options: A way to wrap components in a custom DOM element for styling.
A way to define reusable CSS fragments.
A way to split a component into several files.
A way to group children without creating an extra DOM element.
questions.explanation: Use `<>...</>` or keyed `<Fragment>` when a key is needed.

questions.question: What is reconciliation?
options: Replacing the entire DOM with new HTML on every update.
Fetching fresh data from the server after each render.
React's process of comparing the next element tree with the previous one to determine updates.
Compiling JSX into JavaScript function calls.
questions.explanation: Type, position, and keys affect reuse and state preservation.

questions.question: What is the virtual DOM?
options: An informal term for React's in-memory UI descriptions.
The actual browser DOM tree rendered on the screen.
A separate DOM maintained by the browser for off-screen rendering.
A server-generated HTML snapshot stored for hydration.
questions.explanation: It is not a guarantee that React is always faster than direct DOM code.

questions.question: Why must component names be capitalized in JSX?
options: Because JavaScript requires all function names to be capitalized.
Because lowercase names are reserved for CSS classes.
Because capitalization controls component rendering order.
Uppercase JSX names are treated as component references; lowercase names represent host elements.
questions.explanation: `<Profile />` differs from `<profile />`.

questions.question: What does StrictMode do?
options: It enables production optimizations such as minification.
It forces components to render only on the server.
It disables all warnings in development.
It enables additional development checks to reveal unsafe patterns and lifecycle issues.
questions.explanation: Some renders or Effect setup/cleanup cycles may be repeated in development.

questions.question: Why are keys needed in lists?
options: Keys let React match sibling items across insertions, deletions, and reordering.
Keys make list items render faster by skipping the DOM.
Keys are used to store component state globally.
Keys are required only for items that contain inputs.
questions.explanation: Stable keys preserve the association between logical items and component state.

questions.question: Why can array indexes be bad keys?
options: Array indexes are not allowed as keys by the JSX compiler.
Array indexes make keys too long for React to compare.
When order or membership changes, React may reuse component instances for the wrong items.
Array indexes are always duplicated across lists.
questions.explanation: Index keys are reasonable only for stable lists that do not reorder or change.

questions.question: Is `key` available as a child prop?
options: Yes; it is passed as `props.key` like any other prop.
No, `key` is a special React field and is not passed as a normal prop.
Yes, but only in class components.
Yes, but only when the key is a number.
questions.explanation: Pass the identifier separately if the child needs it.

questions.question: What is conditional rendering?
options: Rendering all components at once and hiding some with CSS only.
Loading components from the server on demand.
Rendering components only on the server.
Rendering different nodes based on expressions or branches.
questions.explanation: Remember that `0 && <Panel />` renders `0`.

questions.question: What is a portal?
options: A component that renders inside an iframe.
A way to render children into a different DOM node while retaining their React-tree context and event propagation.
A way to share state between two separate React apps.
A route that loads content from another URL.
questions.explanation: Useful for dialogs, menus, and overlays.

questions.question: What is an Error Boundary?
options: A component that prevents the user from navigating away from a page.
A hook that validates form input.
A utility that logs errors to the console.
A component boundary that renders fallback UI for eligible descendant rendering errors.
questions.explanation: Traditional boundaries do not catch arbitrary event-handler or async callback errors.

questions.question: How can you reset a component's local state?
options: Call `forceUpdate()` on the component.
Change its `key`, or lift state and reset it explicitly.
Call `useState` again inside the same render.
Set the state variable to `undefined` in an Effect.
questions.explanation: A new key tells React to treat it as a new component identity.

questions.question: What does `{0 && <Widget />}` render?
options: Nothing at all.
It renders `0`.
The text `false`.
The `Widget` component.
questions.explanation: The `&&` operator returns the left operand when it is falsy; React renders numbers.

questions.question: How do you pass a number as a prop?
options: Use an expression such as `count={3}`.
Use quotes such as `count="3"`.
Use a template literal such as `count=`3``.
Numbers cannot be passed as props.
questions.explanation: `count="3"` passes a string.

questions.question: How do inline styles work in JSX?
options: Pass a CSS string, for example `style="margin-top: 8px"`.
Pass a class name through `style={'my-class'}`.
Pass an object, for example `style={{ marginTop: 8, backgroundColor: 'navy' }}`.
Inline styles are not supported in JSX.
questions.explanation: Property names are generally camelCased and numeric units depend on the CSS property.

questions.question: What is the difference between `onClick={save}` and `onClick={save()}`?
options: The first invokes `save` during render; the second passes a handler.
Both pass a handler to the click event.
Both invoke `save` during render.
The first passes a handler; the second invokes `save` during render.
questions.explanation: Invoking during render can trigger unintended work or cause a render loop.

questions.question: Why should you render `<Child />` rather than call `Child(props)`?
options: JSX lets React manage the child as a component with its own identity and Hook call sequence.
Calling `Child(props)` is faster and always preferred.
JSX is required because function calls cannot return elements.
`Child(props)` is not valid JavaScript.
questions.explanation: Direct function calls can break Hook semantics and component boundaries.

questions.question: What happens when a component returns `null`?
options: It renders no UI at that position.
It throws an error.
It renders the text `null`.
It renders an empty `<div>`.
questions.explanation: The component can still participate in the React tree and run eligible logic.

questions.question: Can React render arrays?
options: Yes, arrays of valid React nodes can be rendered.
No; arrays must be wrapped in a `<div>`.
Only arrays of strings can be rendered.
Only arrays of numbers can be rendered.
questions.explanation: Dynamic siblings should have stable keys.

questions.question: Why is `className` used instead of `class`?
options: Because `class` is not allowed in HTML.
Because `className` is faster to render.
Because CSS requires the name `className`.
React DOM JSX uses `className` for the CSS class attribute.
questions.explanation: JSX follows JavaScript syntax conventions.

questions.question: Why should render be pure?
options: Because render must fetch data before returning JSX.
Because render must update the DOM directly.
React may repeat, interrupt, or discard render work; side effects during render can create inconsistent behavior.
Because render runs only once per component.
questions.explanation: Keep external synchronization in event handlers or Effects as appropriate.

questions.question: Why treat state as immutable?
options: Because mutating state is faster than creating new values.
Because state values cannot be objects.
Because React copies mutated state automatically on every change.
Create new arrays or objects rather than mutating existing state.
questions.explanation: Identity changes help React detect updates and preserve predictable rendering.

questions.question: Why might calling `setCount(count + 1)` twice increment only once?
options: Because React ignores the second call.
Both calls can use the same render snapshot of `count`.
Because `setCount` is asynchronous and cancels earlier calls.
Because `count` is a ref and does not update.
questions.explanation: Use `setCount(c => c + 1)` when each update depends on the previous value.

questions.question: What is a functional state update?
options: A setter that accepts a function component.
A setter that is memoized with `useCallback`.
A setter that runs outside of rendering.
A setter callback that receives pending previous state and returns next state.
questions.explanation: It is reliable for queued updates and stale-closure-prone callbacks.

questions.question: Does a state setter change the current variable immediately?
options: No; it queues an update for a subsequent render.
Yes; the variable changes immediately.
Yes, but only inside event handlers.
Yes, if you call `flushSync` first.
questions.explanation: The current render's state remains a snapshot.

questions.question: What is batching?
options: Rendering every state update immediately and separately.
Caching rendered output between renders.
Combining several components into one DOM node.
React processes multiple state updates together to reduce unnecessary renders.
questions.explanation: Modern roots batch many updates, including updates in asynchronous callbacks.

questions.question: What is a controlled input?
options: An input whose value is managed only by the DOM.
An input that cannot be edited by the user.
An input whose current value is driven by React state and an event handler.
An input that is rendered only on the server.
questions.explanation: Use `value` for text inputs and `checked` for checkboxes.

questions.question: What is an uncontrolled input?
options: An input whose value is always driven by React state.
An input that has no `name` attribute.
An input that cannot be submitted in a form.
An input whose current value is managed by the DOM, often accessed through a ref or FormData.
questions.explanation: `defaultValue` sets the initial value without controlling subsequent edits.

questions.question: Why can controlled inputs warn about switching modes?
options: Because controlled inputs cannot have default values.
Because inputs must always be uncontrolled in React.
An input may begin with an undefined value and later receive a defined value.
Because React does not support `value` on inputs.
questions.explanation: Initialize consistently, for example with an empty string, or keep the input uncontrolled.

questions.question: How should a state object field be updated?
options: Mutate the existing field directly and call the setter.
Replace the whole state with a primitive value.
Delete the field and re-add it.
Create a new object and preserve other fields, often with spread syntax.
questions.explanation: State setters replace the state value rather than merging objects automatically.

questions.question: What is state lifting?
options: Moving state into a child component to isolate it.
Storing state in the URL.
Moving shared state to the closest common ancestor of components that need to coordinate.
Copying state into a global variable.
questions.explanation: Pass the value down and callbacks up.

questions.question: When is `useReducer` useful?
options: When state transitions are complex or naturally represented as named actions.
When state is a single boolean.
When you need to fetch data from the server.
When you want to avoid using props.
questions.explanation: Reducers should be pure and must not mutate prior state.

questions.question: What is a stale closure?
options: A callback uses props or state captured by the render in which it was created.
A closure that keeps the component from being garbage collected.
A callback that runs after the component unmounts.
An event handler that is attached twice.
questions.explanation: Use correct dependencies, functional updates, or refs when the intended semantics require it.

questions.question: What is the difference between `preventDefault` and `stopPropagation`?
options: The former stops event propagation; the latter prevents a browser default action.
Both stop event propagation.
The former prevents a browser default action; the latter stops event propagation.
Both prevent a browser default action.
questions.explanation: They solve different problems.

questions.question: How does event bubbling work with portals?
options: Events bubble according to the React tree, even if the portal's DOM node is elsewhere.
Events bubble according to the DOM tree, not the React tree.
Events do not bubble through portals at all.
Events bubble only to the portal container.
questions.explanation: Use propagation controls deliberately when needed.

questions.question: How should multiple form fields be managed?
options: Use a separate `useState` for every field without exception.
Use `document.getElementById` to read each input.
Use named fields to update a state object, or use native form submission and FormData when suitable.
Use a global variable for each field.
questions.explanation: Choose one consistent source of truth for each field.

questions.question: What are the Rules of Hooks?
options: Call Hooks inside loops, conditions, or nested functions.
Call Hooks only in class components.
Call Hooks at the top level of function components or custom Hooks, not conditionally or in loops.
Call Hooks only inside event handlers.
questions.explanation: Stable call order lets React associate Hook state with the correct call.

questions.question: What is `useState`?
options: A Hook that stores data in the browser's local storage.
A Hook that fetches data from a server.
A Hook that runs code after every render.
A Hook that stores local state and returns the current snapshot plus a setter.
questions.explanation: A function initializer supports lazy initialization.

questions.question: What is `useEffect` for?
options: Computing derived values during render.
Handling every user click event.
Declaring component props.
Synchronizing with external systems such as subscriptions, timers, browser APIs, or imperative widgets.
questions.explanation: Do not use Effects merely to calculate values that can be derived during render.

questions.question: When does an Effect cleanup run?
options: Only when the component first mounts.
After every render, before the DOM updates.
Before the Effect re-synchronizes with changed dependencies and when the component unmounts.
Only when the app is closed.
questions.explanation: Development StrictMode may also run an extra setup/cleanup cycle.

questions.question: What does an empty dependency array mean?
options: The Effect runs after every render.
The Effect declares no reactive dependencies and normally runs for that mounted instance, subject to development checks.
The Effect never runs.
The Effect runs only on the server.
questions.explanation: It does not guarantee exactly one setup in every environment.

questions.question: What happens when an Effect dependency is omitted?
options: The Effect always runs only once.
The Effect can use stale values, and the dependency linter may warn.
The component throws a runtime error.
React fills in the missing dependencies automatically.
questions.explanation: Declare reactive dependencies or restructure the code to remove unnecessary ones.

questions.question: When should you avoid an Effect?
options: When you need to subscribe to a WebSocket.
When you need to start a timer.
When deriving render data or handling a user event that can be handled directly in the event handler.
When you need to integrate with a third-party widget.
questions.explanation: Effects are for synchronization with systems outside render.

questions.question: What is `useLayoutEffect`?
options: An Effect that runs after DOM mutations but before repaint, useful for layout measurement.
An Effect that runs before the DOM is updated.
An Effect that runs only on the server.
An Effect that runs only once per app.
questions.explanation: It can block painting, so prefer `useEffect` unless pre-paint work is necessary.

questions.question: What is `useRef`?
options: A state hook that triggers a re-render when changed.
A Hook that subscribes to context changes.
A Hook that memoizes a function.
A persistent mutable container whose changes do not trigger a render.
questions.explanation: Use it for DOM nodes and imperative values such as timer IDs.

questions.question: Why not read or write `ref.current` during render?
options: Refs are mutable and outside the normal reactive render model; render-time access can undermine purity.
Because refs are read-only.
Because refs cannot hold DOM nodes.
Because refs are cleared after every render.
questions.explanation: Use refs in event handlers and Effects for imperative coordination.

questions.question: What is `useMemo`?
options: A performance optimization that caches a calculation while dependencies compare equal.
A Hook that stores state between renders.
A Hook that fetches data lazily.
A Hook that synchronizes with external systems.
questions.explanation: Correctness should not depend on the cache being retained.

questions.question: What is `useCallback`?
options: A Hook that caches a computed value.
A Hook that stores mutable values without rendering.
A Hook that runs an Effect after layout.
A performance optimization that caches a function identity while dependencies compare equal.
questions.explanation: Useful when identity affects memoized children or Hook dependencies, but not needed everywhere.

questions.question: What is `React.memo`?
options: A function that memoizes the component's state.
A hook that caches an Effect.
A component wrapper that can skip rendering when props compare equal by default shallow identity comparison.
A wrapper that renders the component only on the server.
questions.explanation: Own state and context changes can still cause rendering; it is not a semantic guarantee.

questions.question: What is a custom Hook?
options: A function starting with `use` that composes Hooks to reuse stateful logic.
A component that starts with `use`.
A class that extends React.Component.
A utility that reads values from the DOM.
questions.explanation: Each call has its own local state unless it connects to shared state.

questions.question: What does `useContext` do?
options: Creates a new context provider.
Reads values from the URL.
Passes props to a child component.
Reads the nearest provider's value and subscribes the consumer to changes.
questions.explanation: Consumers can update when provider value identity changes.

questions.question: What is `useId` for?
options: Generating stable IDs suitable for accessibility relationships across server and client rendering.
Generating random IDs for list keys.
Generating a new ID on every render.
Storing IDs in local storage.
questions.explanation: Do not use it as a list key or business identifier.

questions.question: What is `useTransition`?
options: Marks updates as urgent so they bypass React's scheduler.
Marks updates as non-urgent and exposes pending state for transition work.
Defers an Effect until the browser is idle.
Cancels in-flight network requests.
questions.explanation: Keep controlled text-input updates urgent.

questions.question: What is `useDeferredValue`?
options: Delays a state update until the next network request.
Allows part of the UI to lag behind a rapidly changing value so expensive rendering can be deferred.
Defers an Effect until the component unmounts.
Debounces input events at the DOM level.
questions.explanation: It does not debounce network requests by itself.

questions.question: What is `useSyncExternalStore`?
options: A Hook for reading context values from multiple providers.
A Hook for safely subscribing to external stores with a snapshot API.
A Hook for synchronizing props with state.
A Hook for managing form state.
questions.explanation: It is designed to integrate external state with concurrent rendering.

questions.question: What is `useEffectEvent` in React 19.2+?
options: It reads context values without subscribing to the provider.
It runs an Effect only once on mount.
It defines a memoized event handler for the DOM.
It defines logic callable from Effects that can read latest props/state without causing Effect resynchronization for those values.
questions.explanation: It is not a general replacement for callbacks or event handlers; verify version support.

questions.question: What does React's `use` API do?
options: It declares a new Hook inside a conditional block.
It runs an Effect synchronously during render.
It reads state from a class component.
It can read supported resources such as Promises or context during render; a pending Promise can suspend.
questions.explanation: Its rules differ from ordinary Hooks, and supported contexts are version-dependent.

questions.question: Why can an Effect fetch display stale results?
options: Because Effects always run in random order.
A slower old request may complete after a newer request and overwrite the result.
Because `fetch` cannot be used inside an Effect.
Because React caches network responses automatically.
questions.explanation: Abort old work where possible or check whether the response is still relevant.

questions.question: Why does StrictMode repeat Effect setup in development?
options: To double the performance of the application.
It tests whether setup and cleanup are correctly symmetrical.
To simulate a slow network connection.
To make sure the Effect runs on the server as well.
questions.explanation: Fix cleanup rather than relying on a fragile run-once ref guard.

questions.question: When is Context a good fit?
options: For frequently changing values such as input text.
For values needed by many descendants, such as theme, locale, or user metadata.
For values used by only one component.
For values that must be shared between separate React apps.
questions.explanation: Context transports values but is not a full state-management strategy by itself.

questions.question: Why can Context trigger many re-renders?
options: Consumers update when the provider value changes identity according to `Object.is`.
Because Context forces every component to re-render on every state change.
Because Context stores values in the DOM.
Because Context always rerenders on the server.
questions.explanation: Split contexts by update frequency or stabilize values when profiling justifies it.

questions.question: What is prop drilling?
options: Passing props from a child up to its parent.
Storing props in a global variable.
Using `useContext` to read props.
Passing props through intermediate components that do not need them solely to reach deeper descendants.
questions.explanation: Composition, Context, or a store can help if they simplify the architecture.

questions.question: How do client state and server state differ?
options: Client state lives on the server; server state lives in the browser.
They are the same and always handled with `useState`.
Server state is only used in class components.
Client state is local UI/application state; server state is remote data with freshness, caching, and synchronization concerns.
questions.explanation: They often need different ownership and invalidation strategies.

questions.question: How do you investigate slow React rendering?
options: Add `React.memo` to every component and measure nothing.
Replace all state with refs.
Remove StrictMode and reload the page.
Profile the interaction with React DevTools, identify expensive renders/calculations, and measure before optimizing.
questions.explanation: Check state placement, unstable props, long lists, and expensive work.

questions.question: What is list virtualization?
options: Rendering all list items off-screen at once.
Paginating the list with server requests.
Rendering only visible list items plus a small overscan region.
Compressing the list's data to reduce memory.
questions.explanation: It reduces DOM work but requires attention to focus, accessibility, and variable row sizes.

questions.question: What is code splitting?
options: Merging all JavaScript files into a single bundle.
Removing unused code from the bundle at build time.
Splitting CSS into separate files per component.
Breaking code into chunks that can be loaded on demand, often by route or feature.
questions.explanation: It reduces initial JavaScript but can add loading boundaries and requests.

questions.question: How does `React.lazy` work?
options: It loads components synchronously at build time.
It converts a class component into a function component.
It memoizes a component's rendered output.
It loads a component from a dynamic import Promise and works with Suspense for pending UI.
questions.explanation: Handle failed imports with an Error Boundary or framework-level mechanism.

questions.question: What is Suspense?
options: A boundary that catches rendering errors and shows a fallback.
A hook that suspends a component's Effects.
A cache for server responses.
A boundary that shows fallback UI while supported child work is not ready.
questions.explanation: It does not automatically catch every arbitrary asynchronous operation.

questions.question: Why is memoization not always faster?
options: Because memoization always makes the first render slower.
It adds comparison, memory, and complexity costs; the original computation may be cheap.
Because memoized values are recomputed on every render.
Because memoization is disabled in production.
questions.explanation: Profile and optimize demonstrated bottlenecks.

questions.question: What is React Compiler?
options: A compiler that converts JSX into plain HTML strings.
A build-time compiler that can automatically memoize safe component computations and functions.
A bundler that replaces Webpack in React apps.
A transpiler that converts class components into hooks at runtime.
questions.explanation: It depends on toolchain configuration and does not excuse impure render logic.

questions.question: How should state location be chosen?
options: Put all state in a single global store.
Use component state for local ephemeral UI, URL state for shareable/navigation state, and shared stores for genuinely cross-cutting state.
Always use component state, regardless of scope.
Always put state in the URL.
questions.explanation: Avoid duplicating the same source of truth in multiple places.

questions.question: What did React 18 introduce at a high level?
options: Server Actions and the App Router.
Class components and PropTypes.
Concurrent rendering capabilities, automatic batching for modern roots, transitions, and expanded Suspense/server-rendering support.
The `useEffectEvent` Hook and the React Compiler.
questions.explanation: Concurrent rendering is a capability, not a promise every render is concurrent.

questions.question: What is `createRoot`?
options: The legacy API for rendering into a DOM node.
An API for creating a server-side stream.
The modern React DOM API for creating a client root.
An API for creating a React Native root.
questions.explanation: It replaced legacy `ReactDOM.render` for modern client entry points.

questions.question: What is `hydrateRoot`?
options: The API that renders a component only on the server.
The API that clears the DOM before rendering.
The API that hydrates server-rendered HTML with client React behavior.
The API that replaces `createRoot` in development.
questions.explanation: Initial client output should match the server markup.

questions.question: What is a Server Component?
options: A component that runs only in the browser and has access to `window`.
A component that must be rendered inside a `<Suspense>` boundary.
A component that stores state in a server-side session.
A component rendered on the server in the React Server Components model and not shipped as ordinary client component code.
questions.explanation: It can access server resources but cannot use client-only Hooks or browser APIs during server rendering.

questions.question: What is a Client Component?
options: A component that runs only on the server and has no access to hooks.
A component that is rendered only during the build.
A component that cannot receive props.
A component marked as a client entry point in an RSC-aware framework, commonly with `'use client'`.
questions.explanation: It can use state, Effects, event handlers, and browser APIs after hydration.

questions.question: What does `'use client'` mean?
options: It marks a function as running on the server.
It enables StrictMode for the module.
It disables server-side rendering for the whole app.
It marks a module as a client entry point in an RSC-aware framework.
questions.explanation: It establishes a client module boundary; not every descendant module needs its own directive.

questions.question: What does `'use server'` mean?
options: It marks a component as a Client Component.
It enables server-side rendering for the module.
It disables client-side JavaScript for the route.
It marks a Server Function/Action in supported React framework setups.
questions.explanation: It does not simply mean the whole file is a Server Component; validate inputs and permissions.

questions.question: What are React Actions?
options: Redux-style objects dispatched to a reducer.
Class component lifecycle methods.
Browser DOM events with custom names.
A model for handling async work and mutations, including APIs such as `useActionState` and `useFormStatus`.
questions.explanation: Frameworks can connect Actions to server execution and cache revalidation.

questions.question: What is `useActionState`?
options: A Hook that manages an Action's result state and exposes a dispatch function and pending state.
A Hook that dispatches Redux actions.
A Hook that reads the browser's history state.
A Hook that stores a mutable ref.
questions.explanation: Check the exact signature for the React version in use.

questions.question: What is `useFormStatus`?
options: A React DOM Hook that reads pending status and related information for a parent form submission.
A Hook that reads the validity of form fields.
A Hook that stores form values in state.
A Hook that submits the form automatically.

It mutates and reuses the same array reference.

questions.question: Why does a log immediately after a state setter show old state?
options: Because `setState` is slow.
Because the log is run before the page loads.
Because state is stored in the DOM.
The current render's state is a snapshot and the setter queues a later render.
questions.explanation: Observe the value in a subsequent render or use a functional update.

questions.question: A child wrapped in `memo` still renders. Why?
options: Props may have new object/function identities, or its own state/context changed.
Because `memo` only works with class components.
Because `memo` is disabled in development.
Because `memo` never compares props.
questions.explanation: Use the Profiler to identify the reason before optimizing.

questions.question: An input's value appears to move to another row after sorting. Why?
options: Because the browser caches input values by position.
Because sorting is not supported with inputs.
Because inputs cannot be rendered inside lists.
Index keys can associate reused component state with the wrong logical item.
questions.explanation: Use a stable data ID as the key.

questions.question: An Effect loops forever. What are likely causes?
options: The Effect has an empty dependency array.
It updates state that changes a dependency, or depends on a newly created object/function each render.
The Effect does not use any state.
The Effect is declared inside a conditional.
questions.explanation: Reconsider the Effect and restructure dependencies rather than blindly suppressing lint.

questions.question: Search results sometimes revert to an old query. Why?
options: A stale network response can finish after a newer response and overwrite it.
Because the browser caches the first response.
Because the server returns results in random order.
Because React does not support async requests.
questions.explanation: Cancel or ignore outdated requests.

questions.question: A Next.js page throws `window is not defined`. What is likely wrong?
options: Browser-only code runs during server evaluation or rendering.
The page is missing a layout.
The page needs `'use server'` at the top.
`window` must be imported from `next`.
questions.explanation: Move it into client-only logic or a targeted client-only import.

questions.question: Dates differ between server and browser. Why?
options: Different time zones or evaluation times produce different initial output.
Because the server and browser always use different locales and time zones by design.
Because dates cannot be serialized.
Because JavaScript Date objects are immutable.
questions.explanation: Render deterministic initial data, then localize after hydration if needed.

questions.question: One user's data appears in another user's page. What should you inspect?
options: Browser extensions installed by the user.
The user's CSS styles.
The image sizes on the page.
Shared cache scope, cache keys, request memoization assumptions, and authorization.
questions.explanation: Personalized data must not leak through shared caches.

questions.question: A mutation succeeds but the page remains stale. What is missing?
options: The mutation must be run twice.
Relevant cache invalidation, revalidation, or refresh after the mutation.
The page needs `'use client'` at the top.
The browser's cookies must be cleared.
questions.explanation: Use the installed version's cache APIs and test affected routes.

questions.question: An input becomes laggy after its state update is wrapped in a transition. Why?
options: Because transitions are disabled for inputs.
Because inputs cannot be rendered in transitions.
Controlled input updates should be urgent, not deferred.
Because transitions always run on the server.
questions.explanation: Update the input synchronously and transition expensive dependent UI.

questions.question: Why can a portal click invoke a React parent handler?
options: Event propagation follows the React tree rather than only physical DOM ancestry.
Because portals copy the handler into the DOM node.
Because portals disable event propagation.
Because the DOM tree is re-created on each click.
questions.explanation: Use `stopPropagation` when appropriate.

questions.question: A server-rendered page is still slow. What do you measure?
options: Only the HTML size.
Only the number of components.
Only the number of Effects.
Server latency, data waterfalls, client JavaScript, hydration, image sizes, cache hits, and Core Web Vitals.
questions.explanation: Server rendering does not eliminate browser work or backend bottlenecks.

questions.question: Design a filtered product listing page. What matters?
options: Store filters in local component state only.
URL-backed filters, pagination semantics, server/client boundaries, cache freshness, loading states, and accessibility.
Fetch all products on the client and filter in the browser.
Use a single hard-coded query.
questions.explanation: Keep shareable state in the URL when useful and avoid duplicated sources of truth.

questions.question: Design an authenticated dashboard. What belongs on the server?
options: Only the UI components and their styles.
Only click handlers and form state.
Session verification, authorization, secret-dependent work, and sensitive data access should remain server-side where possible.
Only animations and transitions.
questions.explanation: Client components can provide interaction but must not be the security boundary.

questions.question: How would you implement optimistic comments?
options: Wait for the server before showing anything.
Reload the page after every comment.
Show a temporary item, submit the mutation, reconcile with the server response, and roll back or mark failure when needed.
Store comments only in the browser.
questions.explanation: Handle duplicate submissions, retries, and ordering.

questions.question: How would you structure a large React codebase?
options: Put all components in one directory.
Organize by feature/domain with clear UI, data, and shared infrastructure boundaries.
Group files by file type, such as all hooks together.
Put every component into a single file.
questions.explanation: Avoid both a giant shared folder and needless abstraction.

questions.question: How would you build robust search-as-you-type?
options: Send a request on every keystroke and show the latest result.
Control request frequency, ignore stale responses, show pending/error/empty states, and consider URL synchronization and accessibility.
Disable the input while requests are in flight.
Fetch all data in advance and filter on the server.
questions.explanation: Transitions can help rendering but do not replace request management.

questions.question: How would you migrate Pages Router to App Router?
options: Rewrite the entire application at once.
Remove the Pages Router and fix errors afterward.
Copy files to the `app` folder without changes.
Migrate incrementally, establish layouts, adapt data fetching, and test routing, caching, authentication, and SEO per route.
questions.explanation: Do not mechanically translate APIs without understanding changed semantics.

questions.question: How would you reduce client JavaScript in Next.js?
options: Mark every component as a Client Component.
Move all logic into `useEffect`.
Use Server Components for server work, minimize client boundaries, inspect bundles, and lazy-load noncritical features.
Bundle all dependencies into one file.
questions.explanation: Measure route-specific bundle and hydration costs.

questions.question: How would you prevent duplicate payment submissions?
options: Disable the submit button forever.
Use only client-side checks.
Enforce idempotency and transactional consistency on the server; make pending/retry behavior clear in the UI.
Refresh the page after the user clicks.
questions.explanation: A disabled button alone cannot guarantee exactly-once processing.

questions.question: How would you design an accessible modal?
options: Use a `<div>` and a `z-index` only.
Use dialog semantics, keyboard support, focus trapping/restoration, Escape behavior, and scroll management.
Ignore keyboard users since modals are visual.
Render the modal without focus management.
questions.explanation: Visual correctness alone is insufficient.

questions.question: How would you cache edited content safely?
options: Clear the entire cache of the app on every request.
Disable caching for all content.
Cache content permanently with no invalidation.
Identify dependent cached data/routes and invalidate the appropriate tags or paths after mutation.
questions.explanation: Test both editor and public views against the chosen cache model.

questions.question: Are React class components still supported?
options: No; they were removed in React 19.
Only in development builds.
Yes, but function components and Hooks are the usual default for new code.
Only inside Next.js.
questions.explanation: Class lifecycles remain relevant in legacy systems and some Error Boundary implementations.

questions.question: What were `getServerSideProps` and `getStaticProps` for?
options: Client-side data fetching and API route handling.
Defining layouts and route groups.
Image optimization and font loading.
Pages Router APIs for request-time server rendering and static generation respectively.
questions.explanation: They are not the primary App Router data-fetching APIs.

questions.question: What is `getStaticPaths`?
options: A Pages Router API that supplies dynamic paths to pre-render with a fallback policy.
A Pages Router API that fetches data on every request.
An API that defines middleware for routes.
An API that configures the build output.
questions.explanation: The App Router commonly uses `generateStaticParams` for related work.

questions.question: What is `next/router` versus `next/navigation`?
options: `next/router` is for the App Router; `next/navigation` is for the Pages Router.
They are identical.
`next/router` is for server code; `next/navigation` is for client code.
`next/router` is for Pages Router; `next/navigation` is for App Router.
questions.explanation: Use the API matching the router in the current file.

questions.question: Why is `ReactDOM.render` legacy?
options: Because it only works on the server.
Because it was never part of React.
Because it cannot render function components.
Modern client roots use `createRoot`, while server-rendered HTML uses `hydrateRoot`.
questions.explanation: Legacy roots do not enable the same modern root behavior.

questions.question: What is the current status of Create React App?
options: It was deprecated for new apps in 2025; current guidance favors a framework or a build tool such as Vite when a framework is not suitable.
It is the recommended default for all new apps.
It was removed from npm.
It is maintained as the official React framework.
questions.explanation: For existing apps, discuss maintenance and migration choices.

questions.question: What should you know about React/Next.js compatibility?
options: Any React version works with any Next.js version.
Next.js ships without React.
React must always be the latest canary release.
Next.js integrates supported React versions; compatibility should be checked against the installed framework release.
questions.explanation: Do not assume every latest React minor works with every Next.js version.

questions.question: Why do React Server Components security advisories matter to Next.js developers?
options: Next.js integrates RSC mechanisms that may be affected by React or protocol vulnerabilities.
They do not affect Next.js because it uses its own renderer.
They only affect React Native apps.
They only affect apps with no server code.
questions.explanation: Keep supported framework and React versions patched and follow official advisories.

questions.question: What changed around params in Next.js 15?
options: `params` was removed completely from the App Router.
`params` became a global variable.
Several App Router request APIs, including `params` and `searchParams`, moved toward asynchronous access; caching defaults also changed.
Caching became permanently disabled.
questions.explanation: Check migration docs for exact behavior.

questions.question: What are Cache Components in Next.js 16?
options: A set of utilities for caching images.
A way to cache only the static assets.
A component library for caching UI.
A newer caching model using explicit cache directives and related rendering behavior, including partial prerendering capabilities.
questions.explanation: Exact setup and semantics are release-specific.
